title: Judges 8:1–3
context: Judges 8:1–3 records a dispute that follows directly on the victory of chapter 7. The men of Ephraim, called in only for the pursuit (7:24), complain sharply that Gideon did not summon them at the start. Gideon answers with humility and a proverb, crediting Ephraim with capturing the princes Oreb and Zeeb, and their anger subsides. The episode shows tribal rivalry threatening Israel’s unity, and it contrasts with Jephthah’s later conflict with the same tribe (12:1–6), which ends in bloodshed.

verses.text: The men of Ephraim said to him, “Why have you treated us this way, that you didn’t call us when you went to fight with Midian?” They rebuked him sharply.
verses.arminianNotes: The Ephraimites ask, “Why have you treated us this way,” and rebuke Gideon “sharply.” Arminian readers note that tribal pride and wounded honor can surface even in the hour of God’s victory. Ephraim’s complaint centers on its own standing rather than on what the LORD has done for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the complaint ignores the plain lesson of chapter 7, that the victory was the LORD’s and not any tribe’s achievement. The same tribe later makes a similar charge against Jephthah (12:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning about pride and rivalry among God’s people, especially after blessing.

verses.text: He said to them, “What have I now done in comparison with you? Isn’t the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon answers, “What have I now done in comparison with you? Isn’t the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?” Arminian readers note Gideon’s wise humility. He defuses the conflict by honoring Ephraim’s contribution above his own clan’s, choosing peace over vindication.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Gideon’s response the wisdom of Proverbs 15:1: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” His proverb exalts the leftovers of Ephraim’s harvest above the full harvest of his own clan. Shared ground: both traditions commend Gideon’s humility here as a model for handling conflict among God’s people.

verses.text: God has delivered into your hand the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb! What was I able to do in comparison with you?” Then their anger was abated toward him when he had said that.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon credits God: “God has delivered into your hand the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb!” Ephraim’s anger subsides. Arminian readers note that Gideon’s answer redirects attention to God’s gift while honoring the Ephraimites’ part, and that their response shows a willingness to be reconciled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reconciliation rests on recognizing God as the giver of victory. When attention turns to what God has done, rivalry loses its force. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a happy resolution, and both note the contrast with Gideon’s harsher treatment of Succoth and Penuel in the next section.
